name: Epistane (Epitiostanol-derivative, Havoc)

lead: Epistane (also Havoc or Epi Plex) is an oral anabolic steroid derived from epitiostanol, a Japanese breast-cancer drug. Lifters use it for muscle gain with less water retention, which they associate with a harder, leaner look.

It is a 17α-methylated androgen from the DHT family, and lab work on human liver cells suggests it raises bile acid synthesis and interacts with nuclear receptors. It appeared in online muscle supplements around 2009. No clinical trials have tested it for muscle or appearance; the literature is chemical analysis of products and a small set of case reports.

paras: It has been sold as an oral over-the-counter-style supplement, typically in capsule form, and used in bodybuilding contexts for a drier, harder look rather than bulk. People using it have commonly paired it with liver-support products, though this has not been studied for it.

A 2020 case series described four users with prolonged cholestasis, and its 17α-methyl group is associated with liver toxicity. It has been a controlled steroid in the US since 2014 under the Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act and is prohibited by WADA.

angle.text: Epistane is used by lifters who want muscle gain with less water, giving a harder, leaner look. It is an androgen-receptor-activating DHT-family steroid sold as a supplement since about 2009; no trials exist, and case reports link it to prolonged cholestasis.

lead: Epistane, also called methylepitiostanol, 17alpha-methylepithiostanol, Havoc or Epi Plex, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from epitiostanol, a compound once used in Japan for breast cancer. It was never marketed as a medicine, but it has been sold online as a bodybuilding supplement since about 2009.[1][2][3]

Analytical chemists identified it in over-the-counter products around 2009 and reported that the ingredient is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list.[2][3] In 2014 it was named among the steroids controlled under the US Designer Anabolic Steroid Control Act.[3]

No controlled trials in healthy users have been published. The main human data are case reports: a 2020 toxicology study described four people who developed long-lasting cholestasis after taking it.[1]

paras: Epistane is a 17alpha-methyl derivative of epitiostanol with a 2alpha,3alpha-epithio ring, and is closely related to mepitiostane. Its formula is C20H32OS.[3] One analytical paper noted it may act as a prodrug of desoxymethyltestosterone.[2]

The compound was first described in the literature in 1974 by Miyake and colleagues and was never developed as a drug.[3] It appeared on the internet in dietary supplements around 2009, sold under names such as Epistane and P-Plex; analysts reported that both ingredients are prohibited in sport.[2] A later review identified it in more than 30 online products that listed it on their labels.[3]

Wikipedia notes that its 17alpha-methyl group is associated with a high potential for liver toxicity.[3] A 2020 study in Archives of Toxicology described four individuals who developed prolonged cholestasis after consuming epistane. In three of them, serum bile acids were raised 14- to 61-fold, and the authors reported laboratory findings that the compound upregulates bile acid synthesis in human liver cells.[1]

Epistane was sold as a supplement ingredient, often described as a 'prohormone' type product, for muscle gain. It is a prohibited substance in sport.[2] In the United States it was added to the list of controlled anabolic steroids in 2014.[3]
No controlled clinical trials have been published. Human evidence is limited to a case series of four people with cholestasis after use.[1]
